reason: The pair is only right when the cartilaginous thing is the lamina itself. Most examples describe the margin or the teeth ('margins cartilaginous', 'cartilaginous teeth'), which belong to the leaf lamina margin and the lamina tooth. A rule would have to move the quality to the margin or tooth when the text names it. A lamina that is cartilaginous in texture (some succulents and conifer leaves) is real.

A floral disc can be papillate, tuberculate or papillose. PATO texture is the attribute, and the value terms (papillose, tuberculate) should be the more specific quality when they exist. Negated 'not papillose' must stay a negation.
Sepal margins are often entire, and the examples are correct. Check that PATO_0104359 is the margin-entire value and not an unrelated 'entire' (for example a whole organ).

A whole plant is not 'soft' in a single sense. The examples read 'plant base soft', 'bases soft' and 'soft-wooded', so they describe a part (base, wood). Softness belongs on that part. A rule would send 'soft' to the named part.

Sepals can be asymmetric. The examples 'inequilateral' and 'base inequilateral' look like leaf-blade wording and may sit on the wrong part. A rule would need the bearer to be a sepal in the text, not a leaf.

Examples such as 'all parts obliquely ascending' do not describe a pinna. A pinna is a leaflet of a pinnate leaf and its orientation is not normally 'ascending' in this sense, so the pair comes from a wrong bearer reading. Pinnae can be ascending in a few ferns, but the text does not show that.

A seed can be large, and PATO_0000586 is increased size. Examples such as 'much larger than congenerics' are comparative and correct. Absolute 'large' is acceptable under the existing size convention.
A pedicel can droop, nod or be pendulous. The examples match drooping.
A stipule can be narrow, so decreased width fits. The example 'apex narrow' belongs to the apex and not to the stipule, but the main pair is correct.
Lateral veins can be raised on a leaf surface, so this is correct. A surface (abaxial or adaxial) is often given, which belongs to a separate qualifier.
Glands (secretory tissue) can be small, and the examples are correct.
A leaf lamina can be soft (texture), and the examples describe the blade.
Corolla lobes can be papillate, which is a surface texture, and the examples are correct.

A labellum lobe has a shape, but the examples mix in the margin ('margins erose'), the apex ('apex acute') and other leaf-like shapes. A rule would have to separate the whole lobe's shape from the margin or apex shape, which belong on their own parts.

Hyaline or scarious involucral bract margins are common, but the quality belongs to the margin and not the whole bract. PATO transparent is acceptable for a hyaline structure. A rule would need the margin as bearer, so a statement about the margin is not moved to the bract.
Perigynia of sedges (Carex) are ascending or spreading on the spike, so the pair is correct.

A petal can be fimbriate, but the examples are mostly 'margins fimbriate', so the quality belongs to the petal margin. A rule would put it on the margin when a margin is stated and on the petal when it is not.
The examples ('3-5 mm deep') almost certainly give the depth of a lobe, sinus or tube, not of the flower. Depth is a measure of an indentation, so it does not belong to the flower as a whole.
An orchid labellum can be papillose or tuberculate. These are texture states and the examples are correct.
Roots can spread (taproots, horizontally spreading roots), so the pair is correct.
A moss seta can be smooth or rough, and the examples are correct.
Bipartite petals (cut into two parts to near the base) are real, for example in Caryophyllaceae. The French examples are correct.
Terete (cylindrical) leaf blades are common in Juncus, Allium and others, so the pair is correct.
Inflorescence branches can be glabrous, and the examples are correct.
Chestnut brown seeds fit red brown, and a seed colour is correct. If a chestnut-brown value term exists, use it instead.

Emarginate describes a notched apex. The examples ('apex emarginate') show the quality belongs to the lobe apex, and corolla lobes can be emarginate. A rule would need to keep the apex as the bearer when it is named.
A floral disc has a shape (annular, tubular, cushion-shaped). The example 'with multiple longitudinal ribs' is a different feature, but the pair is meaningful.
Internodes can be short, and PATO_0000574 is decreased length. The examples are correct.
A perigynium has a 2-D shape (ovate, elliptic). The examples include 'apex rounded or obtuse', which is an apex shape and not the perigynium. A rule would send apex statements to the apex.

A utricle can be longer than another part, which is a ratio comparison. The pair is correct as a comparative length, but the 'longer than glume' pattern should be treated as a relation to another part (ratio pattern).
Bracts, including phyllaries, can be sericeous (silky hairs), and the examples are correct.
The examples are 'apex tapering to beak', which describe the perigynium apex and not the whole organ. The whole perigynium can taper, but a rule would need to attach it to the apex when one is named.
Lateral veins can be impressed (sunken) on the adaxial surface, so the pair is correct.

A peristome tooth has a shape (linear, lanceolate, subulate). The examples include 'obtuse at the apex' and 'keeled at back', which describe a part or feature of the tooth. A rule would need to separate whole-tooth shape from apex.

A short shoot in the examples is likely a wrong reading. The sizes '4.5-7 x 2-4 mm' and '1 mm wide' seem to be about leaves or needles, and 'short shoot' may come from a generic phrase. A short shoot can have a width, but the examples do not support the pair.
Anthers or their locules can be subglobose, which maps to spheroid. The examples are acceptable.

A floral disc can have a diameter, but the examples include 'disk glands ca. 0.5 mm in diam.', which describe the glands and not the disc. A rule would need to check which part the measurement belongs to.
Cuneate describes the base of a pinnule, not the whole pinnule. The pair is meaningful only when the base is the described region. A rule would need to keep the base as bearer.
Achenes can be obovate, and the examples are correct.

The examples are about perichaetial leaves of mosses that are differentiated from other leaves. It is a comparison with other leaves, not an intrinsic quality. It is valid only for the bryophyte perichaetial leaf, not for any leaf. A rule would need the perichaetial context.
A fruit can have a colour (straw-coloured), and the examples are correct. A more specific colour value should be used if one exists.
Achenes can be glossy or shiny, and glistening is a reasonable PATO match.
Leaf lamina teeth can be obtuse, and the examples are correct.
Involucral bracts or lobes can be triangular, and the examples are correct.
The number of achenes is a count, so amount fits. The example 'in 12 vertical rows' is a row count and not an achene count, but the pair is meaningful.
Leaf laminas can be lanate (woolly) on a face, and the examples are correct.

PATO_0000001 (quality) is a very general root term. The examples ('stout or slender', 'simple or bifurcate', 'stipitate-glandular') are unrelated qualities, so the pair is too vague and should be mapped to specific terms.
A pedicel can be hispid (stiff bristly hairs), and the examples are correct.

A corolla lip can be spurred, but the spur is a separate structure (a spur on the lip base). The pair is meaningful only as a shorthand for 'has a spur', so a rule would need to give it as a part (spur) and not as a quality.
A leaf rachis can have a colour, and the examples are correct. A hair colour (fulvous puberulous) belongs to the indumentum and not the rachis, but the pair is meaningful.
Latex has a colour (white, orange, red), and the examples are correct.

The examples ('solitary in an involucral bract sheath', 'many flowered') describe the number or arrangement of flowers, not the spike inflorescence. Spatial pattern may fit an arrangement along the spike, but a rule would need to separate count from arrangement.
A plant spore has a size in micrometres, and the examples give length x width. Width is correct for the second dimension.
A megasporangiate strobilus (female cone) has a colour (purple, brown), and the examples are correct.
A perianth tube has a length, and the examples give lengths in mm or cm. Examples like '11-16 x 11-16 mm' may be a different part, but the pair is meaningful.
Pinnae can be asymmetric or inequilateral, which is common in ferns and pinnate leaves, and the examples are correct.
Secondary leaf veins can be raised on one or both surfaces, and the examples are correct.
A short shoot can be thick, but 'large and thick' and 'thickened toward end' may describe a different organ (spur or leaf). A rule would need to check that the bearer is the short shoot.

A rhizome covered with fibrils or fibres is plausible. However, 'fibrillose' describes the covering (scales, fibres) and not the rhizome itself. A rule would need to treat it as a surface texture and not as a part.
A leaf lamina can be carinate (keeled), and the examples are correct. The 'not carinate' example must be kept as a negation.
